questions.stem: Abdul, 30, is rocking in his chair at a GP clinic, holding the left side of his head. He has had a severe left orbital headache at about 7 am almost every day for 2 months. He has no nausea and no aura. You want one history question that best helps tell cluster headache from migraine. Which question is it?
options: "Does the pain have a throbbing or pulsing quality to it?"
"During an attack, do you lie still in a dark room or move about?"
"Does the headache ever wake you up from your sleep?"
"Have you found that paracetamol helps with the pain?"
questions.why: Behaviour during an attack is a key discriminator. People with cluster headache are restless: they pace, rock or even bang their head. People with migraine lie still, because movement makes the pain worse. Restlessness or agitation is one of the ICHD-3 criteria for cluster headache.
notes: Throbbing pain is common in both migraine and cluster headache, so it doesn't separate them.
Migraine can also wake people from sleep. Waking needs exploring as a possible red flag, but it doesn't tell cluster headache apart from migraine.
Simple analgesics often fail in both conditions, so the answer doesn't separate them.

questions.stem: Abdul, 30, has episodic cluster headache with a normal ECG and normal MRI brain. He comes to the GP clinic 15 minutes into a typical left orbital attack and wants relief now. Which acute treatment is most appropriate?
options: Oxygen 2 L/min via nasal prongs for 15 minutes
Oral sumatriptan 50 mg, repeated after 2 hours if needed
100% oxygen at 12 to 15 L/min via non-rebreather mask for 15 minutes
Oral ibuprofen 400 mg with paracetamol 1 g
questions.why: High-flow 100% oxygen at 12 to 15 L/min through a non-rebreather for 15 minutes aborts many cluster attacks. Subcutaneous sumatriptan 6 mg is the other first-line option. Oral drugs act too slowly for attacks that peak quickly.
notes: Low-flow oxygen through nasal prongs doesn't deliver a high enough concentration to abort a cluster attack.
Oral triptans are absorbed too slowly to help a cluster attack. The subcutaneous (6 mg) or intranasal route is needed.
Simple oral analgesics don't work for cluster attacks, and Abdul has already found paracetamol useless.

questions.stem: During his attacks, Abdul, 30, has a watering red left eye and a runny, blocked left nostril, on the same side as his left orbital pain. What mechanism best explains these features?
options: Trigeminal-autonomic reflex driving parasympathetic outflow via the facial nerve
Sympathetic overactivity from the superior cervical ganglion on the left side
Passive fluid leak from venous congestion of the left cavernous sinus
Mast cell histamine release in the left nasal and conjunctival mucosa
questions.why: Pain input from the trigeminal nerve activates the superior salivatory nucleus. Parasympathetic fibres then travel via the facial nerve (greater petrosal nerve) and pterygopalatine ganglion to the lacrimal gland and nasal mucosa, causing tearing, redness and rhinorrhoea on the same side.
notes: Tearing and nasal secretion are parasympathetic functions. In cluster headache the sympathetic supply is actually underactive, which is why a partial Horner's syndrome appears.
Venous congestion of the cavernous sinus doesn't explain active glandular secretion, and Abdul's MRI showed normal cavernous sinuses.
Histamine release from mast cells is the mechanism of allergic rhinoconjunctivitis. It doesn't explain strictly one-sided features tied to a pain attack.

questions.stem: During an attack, Abdul, 30, has mild drooping of his left upper eyelid and a small left pupil. Both resolve once the attack settles. This is a partial Horner's syndrome. Loss of sympathetic supply to which muscle causes the mild ptosis?
questions.why: The superior tarsal (Müller's) muscle is smooth muscle with a sympathetic supply. It adds a few millimetres of upper lid elevation, so sympathetic loss gives only mild ptosis. Complete ptosis points to the levator and the oculomotor nerve.
notes: The levator palpebrae superioris is supplied by the oculomotor nerve. Paralysis of it causes marked or complete ptosis, not the mild droop of Horner's.
The orbicularis oculi closes the eyelids and is supplied by the facial nerve. Weakness of it causes incomplete eye closure, not ptosis.
The inferior tarsal muscle helps hold down the lower lid. Losing its supply slightly raises the lower lid, so it doesn't cause the upper lid droop.
